work-by-forces-s1.title: A crate pulled across a rough floor
work-by-forces-s1.html: The crate starts from rest. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

work-by-forces-s2.title: A stretched band launches a cart
work-by-forces-s2.text: A stretched elastic band pushes a 0.60 kg cart along a level, low-friction track. The graph shows the band's force on the cart, in the direction of motion, against the cart's position. The cart starts from rest at x = 0.

items.q: How much work does the rope do on the crate over the 4.00 m? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that uses the whole rope force. Only the part along the displacement does work: F d cos 30°.
Value: that uses sin 30°. The angle is measured from the displacement, so use cos 30°.

why.correct: W = F_T d cos θ = (45.0 N)(4.00 m)(cos 30°) = 156 J. The angle is between the force and the displacement.

items.q: How much work does kinetic friction do on the crate over the 4.00 m, in joules? Include the sign.

why.correct: Friction points opposite the displacement (θ = 180°), so W = f_k d cos 180° = −(28.0 N)(4.00 m) = −112 J.

items.q: How much work do the normal force and the gravitational force do on the crate over the 4.00 m?
options: Zero each, because each is perpendicular to the displacement
+696 J by the normal force and −784 J by gravity
Zero by the normal force, −784 J by gravity
Both positive, since both act on the crate while it moves

why.correct: Both forces are vertical and the crate moves horizontally, so θ = 90° and W = Fd cos 90° = 0 for each.
options: Right: cos 90° = 0, so a force at right angles to the motion does no work.
These multiply each force by 4.00 m as if it pointed along the motion. Both are vertical; the motion is horizontal.
Gravity is also perpendicular to the horizontal displacement, so it does no work here.
A force does work only through its component along the displacement. Both of these have none.

items.q: What is the net work done on the crate over the 4.00 m, in joules?

mistakes.why: Value: that adds the friction work as if it were positive. Friction does negative work, so subtract it.
Value: that uses the whole rope force (180 J). The rope does F d cos 30° = 156 J.

why.correct: W_net = 155.9 J + (−112 J) + 0 + 0 = 43.9 J. By the work-energy theorem this is also the crate's change in kinetic energy.

items.q: The crate starts from rest. How fast is it moving after the 4.00 m, in m/s?

mistakes.why: Value: that uses only the rope's work. The change in kinetic energy equals the net work, so include friction.

why.correct: Work-energy theorem: W_net = ΔK = ½mv² − 0, so v = √(2W_net/m) = √(2 × 43.9 J / 20.0 kg) = 2.09 m/s.

items.q: How much work does the band do on the cart from x = 0 to x = 0.40 m, in joules?

mistakes.why: Value: that treats the force as 12 N the whole way. The work is the area under the graph, and the force falls after 0.10 m.
Value: that treats the whole area as one triangle. From 0 to 0.10 m it is a rectangle.

why.correct: Work is the area under the force-position graph: rectangle (12 N)(0.10 m) = 1.2 J plus triangle ½(12 N)(0.30 m) = 1.8 J, so 3.0 J.

items.q: How fast is the 0.60 kg cart moving at x = 0.40 m, in m/s?

mistakes.why: Value: that uses 4.8 J, a constant 12 N force. Use the area under the graph, 3.0 J.

why.correct: The band is the only force doing work along the track, so ΔK = 3.0 J: v = √(2 × 3.0 J / 0.60 kg) = √10 m/s = 3.2 m/s.

items.q: What happens to the cart's speed between x = 0.40 m and x = 0.50 m?
options: It decreases, because the band no longer pushes
It stays the same, because the band does no work there
It increases, because the cart is still moving forward
It drops to zero, because the force is zero

why.correct: Between 0.40 m and 0.50 m the force is zero, so the work is zero and, by the work-energy theorem, ΔK = 0: the speed stays at 3.2 m/s.
options: With no force (and low friction) nothing slows the cart. Velocity changes need a net force.
Right: the force is zero, so no work is done and K does not change.
Moving forward does not add energy. The speed rises only while positive work is done.
Zero force means zero acceleration, not zero speed. The cart keeps the speed it has.

items.q: Over which 0.10 m interval does the band do the most work on the cart?
options: Each of the four intervals, equally

why.correct: Areas: 0-0.10 m: 1.2 J; 0.10-0.20 m: 1.0 J; 0.20-0.30 m: 0.6 J; 0.30-0.40 m: 0.2 J. The cart gains kinetic energy fastest at the start.
options: The force starts to fall here, so the area is 1.0 J, a little less than the first interval.
The force is smallest here; the area is only 0.2 J.
Right: 1.2 J, the largest area, because the force is largest there.
The intervals have the same width but different force heights, so the areas differ.

items.q: A worker lowers a 15 kg box onto the floor at constant speed. What sign is the work done by the worker on the box?
options: Positive, because the worker is making an effort
Zero, because the speed is constant
Positive, because the box moves
Negative, because the worker pushes up while the box moves down

why.correct: The worker's force on the box is upward and the displacement is downward (θ = 180°), so the worker does negative work. Gravity does an equal amount of positive work, so the net work is zero and the speed is constant.
options: Work in physics is F d cos θ, not effort. Here the force opposes the motion.
Constant speed means the net work is zero. The worker's own work is negative, balancing gravity's positive work.
Motion alone does not fix the sign. The angle between the force and the displacement does.
Right: force and displacement are opposite, so cos 180° = −1.

items.q: A ball on a string moves in a horizontal circle at constant speed. Which is the best explanation of why its speed does not change?
options: The string's force is perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work
The string's force is zero, because the ball moves at constant speed
The string does positive work that is cancelled by negative work from gravity
The ball has no acceleration, so nothing does work

why.correct: The tension points to the center and the velocity is tangent to the circle, so θ = 90° at every instant: W = 0, ΔK = 0, and the speed stays the same.
options: Right: a force at 90° to the motion changes the direction but adds no kinetic energy.
The string pulls toward the center; without it the ball would not turn.
Gravity is vertical and the circle is horizontal, so gravity does no work either.
The ball accelerates toward the center. The point is that this force does no work.

items.q: A 3.0 kg ball falls 2.5 m. How much work does the gravitational force do on the ball, in joules? Use g = 9.8 m/s².

why.correct: The gravitational force (mg, down) and the displacement (2.5 m, down) point the same way, so W = mgd = (3.0 kg)(9.8 m/s²)(2.5 m) = 74 J.

items.q: A car drives up a straight hill at constant speed. What is the net work done on the car?
options: Positive, because the engine pushes the car uphill
Zero, because its kinetic energy does not change
Negative, because gravity opposes the motion
It equals the car's weight times the height of the hill

why.correct: Constant speed means ΔK = 0, so by the work-energy theorem the works done by all the forces add to zero.
options: The road's push does positive work, but gravity does an equal amount of negative work.
Right: the work-energy theorem says W_net = ΔK, and ΔK = 0.
Gravity does negative work, but the forward push from the road balances it.
That is the size of the work done by gravity alone, not the net work.

items.q: A 0.17 kg puck slides at 6.0 m/s onto rough ice, where a 0.50 N friction force slows it. How far does it slide before stopping, in meters?

mistakes.why: Value: that divides mass times speed by the force. Use the work-energy theorem: −f d = 0 − ½mv².

why.correct: Friction does all the work: −f d = 0 − ½mv², so d = mv²/(2f) = (0.17 kg)(6.0 m/s)²/(2 × 0.50 N) = 6.1 m.

items.q: A crate is dragged 5.0 m east and then 5.0 m back west to where it started. Kinetic friction from the floor has size f the whole time. What total work does friction do on the crate?
options: Zero, because the crate ends where it started

why.correct: On each leg friction points opposite the displacement: W = −f(5.0 m) twice, for −f(10 m). The work done by friction depends on the path length, not just the start and end.
options: The displacement is zero overall, but friction reverses with the motion, so it does negative work on each leg.
Friction always acts against the sliding, so its work on the crate is negative.
Right: friction opposes the motion on both legs, so each leg contributes −f(5.0 m).
That counts one leg. The return trip adds the same negative work again.

items.q: A constant force pushes a cart along its motion. If the force is doubled and the distance is halved, what happens to the work done by the force?
options: It doubles
It is halved
It is four times as large
It stays the same

why.correct: W = Fd, so (2F)(d/2) = Fd: the work is unchanged.
options: Doubling the force doubles the work only at the same distance; halving the distance cancels it.
The force also changes; the two factors cancel.
This multiplies by 2 twice. One factor is 2 and the other is ½.
Right: W = Fd, and 2 × ½ = 1.

items.q: On a graph of the force along the direction of motion against position, what represents the work done by the force?
options: The area between the graph and the position axis
The slope of the graph
The largest force times the total time
The height of the graph at the final position

why.correct: Work equals the area under a force-position graph, with area below the axis counting as negative work.
options: Right: each thin strip F Δx is a little work, and they add up to the area.
Slope is a change in force per meter, not an amount of energy.
Work is force times displacement, not force times time.
That is one force value, in newtons, not an energy in joules.

items.q: Take a sled as the system. A rope outside the system pulls it forward and does +40 J of work on it. What does this tell you?
options: 40 J of energy left the sled
40 J of energy entered the sled system across its boundary
The sled's speed is certain to increase
The rope gained 40 J

why.correct: Work by an external force is energy crossing the system boundary: +40 J means 40 J entered the sled. Whether the sled speeds up depends on the net work of all the forces.
options: Positive work brings energy in; negative work takes it out.
Right: positive work by an external force is an energy transfer into the system.
The net work decides the change in speed. Other forces, such as friction, may do negative work.
The rope gave energy to the sled; it did not gain it.
